title: The Lotus Sutra — the Sanskrit text
textType: Mahayana sutra in prose and verse
attributionNote: A Mahayana sutra transmitted without an author and presented as the Buddha's own teaching on the Vulture Peak, assembled in the early centuries of the common era from layers of older verse and prose. GRETIL's e-text follows P. L. Vaidya's edition (Darbhanga 1960, Buddhist Sanskrit Texts 6) and was input by the Digital Sanskrit Buddhist Canon Input Project.
description: The Saddharmapuṇḍarīkasūtra teaches that there is one vehicle and not three, that the Buddha's own awakening is immeasurable in age, and that a Buddha's lifespan and skilful means are beyond the measure of his hearers: the parable of the burning house and the three carts, the parable of the prodigal son, the jewelled stupa that opens to reveal the Buddha of the distant past, the dragon king's daughter who attains awakening, and the Bodhisattva Never Disparaging who salutes every being as a future Buddha. Its chapters on the duration of the Buddha's life and on the universal capacity to attain Buddhahood became the doctrinal centre of East Asian Buddhism.
historicalContext: Composed in India and carried to China by Kumārajīva's translation of 406 and to Tibet later, the sutra was the ground of the Tiantai and Tendai schools and of the Japanese devotion to the Lotus that gave rise to Nichiren. Its Sanskrit text survives in Nepalese manuscripts and in the Central Asian fragments that the Vaidya edition collects.
availabilityNote: Complete as GRETIL publishes it: all twenty-seven parivartas with their prose and verse, 1,230 passages, streamed from GRETIL at read time, one chapter at a time. This is the original Sanskrit, not a translation; the library holds Kern's English translation of the same sutra as The Lotus Sutra.
